questions.question: Define mass movement precisely and explain the balance of forces on a slope, including water's double role and the main natural and human triggers.
questions.expected_answer: Mass movement or mass wasting is the movement of weathered material downslope under the direct pull of gravity, without a transporting agent such as a river, glacier or wind — gravity as driver and the absence of a transporting medium are both essential to the definition. Stability is a contest between driving forces, chiefly gravity's downslope pull which grows with slope angle, and resisting forces — friction, the interlocking of particles, dry cohesion and plant roots binding the soil. Water plays a double role: small amounts bind material, as damp sand binds a sandcastle, but saturation fills the pores and pushes particles apart, adds weight and lubricates potential slide surfaces such as the soil-bedrock junction, which is why most disasters follow heavy or prolonged rain. Other triggers are undercutting of the slope base by rivers, waves or road cuttings, which removes support where it matters most; earthquakes and blasting; freeze-thaw prying rock from cliffs; and human actions — stripping vegetation, loading slopes with buildings and dumps, leaking water into slopes, and cutting steep unsupported faces.

questions.question: Describe the six kinds of mass movement on the speed-and-water ladder, with the field evidence or setting that identifies each.
questions.expected_answer: Soil creep is the slowest: the soil blanket migrates millimetres per year as wetting-drying and heating-cooling cycles lift particles at right angles to the slope and settle them slightly downhill; it is identified by tilted fence posts and gravestones, curved tree trunks, terracettes and soil piled against the upslope side of walls. Solifluction is creep's cold wet cousin: in mountains where the subsoil freezes, the thawed waterlogged surface layer flows slowly over the frozen layer beneath in lobes, as on the high Drakensberg and Lesotho slopes. Landslides are rapid: a coherent mass slides along a defined, broadly planar surface, usually after saturation, commonly where a road cutting exposes strata parallel to the slope. A slump is a rotational slide along a curved spoon-shaped surface, leaving a crescent scar above and a backward-tilted block below, typical of thick soils and embankments. Rock falls are free-fall: blocks pried from cliffs by freeze-thaw drop, bounce and shatter, feeding the talus. Mud flows are the fastest and wettest: soil and debris so saturated they behave as a fluid, racing down valleys and setting like concrete, deadliest on deforested or burnt slopes after cloudbursts. The ladder runs creep, solifluction, landslide, slump, rock fall, mud flow — speed rising, and water content rising from slide to flow.

questions.question: Analyse the April 2022 KwaZulu-Natal disaster as a case study of mass movement impacts, and set out the prevention and minimisation strategies with South African examples.
questions.expected_answer: In April 2022, over 300 millimetres of rain fell in 24 hours across parts of the Durban metro — months of rain in a day. Saturated, steep coastal hillsides failed in hundreds of places at once: landslides and mud flows tore through formal and informal settlements, more than 400 people died, thousands of homes were destroyed, and roads, rail, the harbour and water systems suffered billions of rands in damage. The analysis must include vulnerability: losses concentrated where poverty had pushed informal settlement onto steep unstable slopes with cut unsupported platforms, stripped vegetation, leaking water and no drainage — the rain was general but the risk was unequal. Environmental impacts of mass movement generally include stripped slopes, buried topsoil and sediment-choked rivers and dams. Strategies group into four families: engineering the slope — regrading to gentler angles, terracing, retaining walls and gabions at the toe, rock anchors, mesh and catch fences, with Chapman's Peak Drive's fences, anchored mesh and half-tunnel as the showcase; managing water — cut-off drains above the slope, subsurface drains, sealed cracks and repaired pipes, and never discharging stormwater onto a slope face; protecting the surface — keeping and restoring vegetation whose roots bind soil, re-greening burnt or cleared slopes, controlling grazing; and planning — GIS hazard mapping overlaying slope, soil, drainage and rainfall, keeping housing off high-risk slopes, enforcing regulations on cuttings, rainfall-triggered early warnings as Durban has introduced since 2022, community education on warning signs such as fresh cracks, leaning poles, jamming doors and new seepage, and upgrading or dignified relocation of settlements already on dangerous ground.
